Chapter 7: Humility and Confidence—A New Way to Hold Faith
There’s a quiet power in humility—even if it’s often misunderstood. Some folks think humility means you have to shrink back, downplay what you believe, or avoid speaking up. But true humility? It’s different. It’s about holding your convictions with open hands, being honest about what you don’t know, and always being willing to grow.
Let me share a story. There was this high school coach—steady, reliable, the kind of person people gravitate toward. One day, a student asked him, “Why do you still believe in God when so many smart people don’t?” The coach just smiled and said, “I’ve learned a lot over the years, but I haven’t learned everything. I believe because I’ve seen too much beauty and meaning to think this is all just an accident. But I’m always open to learning more.” The student was taken aback—not because the coach had all the answers, but because he was honest.
Most of us don’t realize that humility and confidence can actually work together. You know, the loudest voices in debates often sound so sure of themselves. But real confidence? It’s quieter. It’s the kind that knows your faith isn’t threatened by tough questions, and you don’t have to act like you know it all.
That coach’s way of responding really stuck with people. He didn’t try to win with arguments or brush aside doubts. Instead, he showed what it looks like to be both grounded and open. And you know what? Over time, more students came to talk to him—not because he could solve every problem, but because he was willing to listen and walk alongside them.
What’s amazing is how clear it becomes: humility isn’t weakness. It’s actually the soil where real confidence grows. When you’re not afraid to admit what you don’t know, you’re free—to keep searching, to keep learning, and to invite others along for the ride.
So if you ever feel pressure to have it all figured out, here’s some good news. You don’t have to pick between humility and conviction. You can hold both. And when you do, you become someone others trust—not because you’re always right, but because you’re genuine.
